newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France to reveal winner of Thomson bid soon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France to reveal winner of Thomson bid soon.

text.p: Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Tuesday that the government would decide in the next few days to whom it would sell electronics giant Thomson SA.

He told parliament reports that a decision had been taken were "beyond the truth", but his remarks failed to dampen bourse speculation that boosted trade in the shares of the two bidders, Alcatel Alsthom and Lagardere Groupe. Alcatel shares closed down 2.22 percent at 444.90 francs on rumours its bid would prevail.
One trader said it was rumoured the government would announce on Tuesday evening that Alcatel's bid had won, but Thomson's missiles operations would be sold to Lagardere.
Lagardere closed up 2.94 percent at 133.10 francs.
Lagardere, Alcatel and Thomson officials declined comment.
"The government will take a decision on the privatisation of Thomson in the coming days," Arthuis said during question time in parliament.
Asked if the government had decided to sell the company to Alcatel, he said those reports went "beyond the truth."
A decision had been expected as early as Monday as the sale of Thomson will have a profound effect on the French electronics and defence industries.
Thomson owns Thomson Multimedia, one of the world's leading television makers and 58 percent of Thomson-CSF, which ranks among the world's five biggest defence electronics companies.
Lagardere and Alcatel have described the broad outlines of their business plans for Thomson, but not the financial details or amounts of their bids.

Lagardere, a conglomerate with interests ranging from media to defence, would control Thomson-CSF, but sell minority holdings to British Aerospace Plc, GEC Plc and perhaps Daimler-Benz Aerospace GmbH (DASA).
It has lined up South Korea's Daewoo to run Thomson Multimedia. Daewoo's chairman said he saw synergies in the components businesses and promised to create jobs in France.

Alcatel Alsthom wants to turn Thomson-CSF into the second-most important defence company after Lockheed Martin, but ahead of GM Hughes Electronics Corp. It plans a "wide-scale partnership with another major industrial player" in Britain, Germany or both to achieve that goal.
French newspapers speculate the state may have to pump billions of francs into Thomson prior to the sale. It lost 1.379 billion francs and has 25 billion francs of debt.
Thomson Multimedia lost 1.09 billion francs, but Thomson-CSF posted a 1.01 billion profit in 1995.

Arthuis did not say if the state would inject money into Thomson before the sale, but said that previous refusals were among the reasons for the company's troubles. The state directly owns 76 percent of Thomson and 20 percent through state telecommunications operator France Telecom.
